meta.blurb: Ilse Quill mends maps and never leaves home after dark. Then a sea captain asks her to read a thief's old chart and steal the one map that could feed a hungry island. Ilse would much rather stay and drink her tea.
meta.bible: Ilse Quill: a nervous, tidy map-mender of Lanternhaven; loves tea, ink and a locked door by sunset; sharp-eyed and stubborn when it matters. Mistress Pim: the baker next door, warm and talkative. Captain Odalys Brae: tall, salt-stained, born on Kettle Island; her mother still lives there. Fenwick: the big, gentle cook of the barge; ginger tea cures seasickness. Tamsin Pike: fifteen, the engineer, always has oil on her hands. Barnaby Hatch: the old navigator, half blind, knows water by smell and sound. Corvin Ashgrove: the Harbour Lord, smooth and greedy, sells safe passage through the reef. Gull's Patience: the patched barge with one mast and a small steam engine. Lanternhaven: the harbour city of lamps. Kettle Island: a hungry island whose boats cannot pass the reef. Whisperreef: a maze of pale stone teeth and channels that change with the tide; it whispers in the wind. Grey Breath: the fog bank on the reef. Tide-Gate: a stone arch that opens only at low tide. Skerry Hollow: the black rock where the tower stands. Glass Tower: the Harbour Lord's tower of mirrored windows. Warden Herons: clockwork birds that guard the tower and move to a steady click. Moon Atlas: the only chart of the safe channels; its ink shows only in moonlight. Jory Lightfoot: a famous thief of long ago whose pinholed map Ilse reads. Pinholes: tiny holes in the paper that make a hidden route. Lamp-eels: glowing eels that swarm to lamplight. Voice and tone: warm, wry and gently funny, with real danger and no gore; Ilse is brave in spite of herself.

B1B2: Rain is running down the window of the little shop where Ilse Quill mends maps. She is humming quietly, because the tear in front of her is almost fixed.
Ilse has a rule that she is always home before the lamps are lit. She has never sailed on a ship, and she has never wanted to.
Mistress Pim brings a warm loaf from next door and shakes her head sadly. Nobody from Kettle Island has come to the market for weeks, and the price of flour keeps rising.
The door bangs open and a tall woman in a salt-stained coat stands dripping on the mat. She is Captain Odalys Brae, and she is carrying an old map rolled under her arm.
When Ilse lifts the paper to the lamp, hundreds of tiny holes shine like stars. She realises that this is no ordinary map, because someone has pricked a secret route through it.

The only safe way through the Whisperreef is shown in the Moon Atlas, the captain explains, and Harbour Lord Corvin Ashgrove keeps it locked away. He sells passage at a price that Kettle Island can never pay.
Captain Brae says that only a map-mender could read the thief's secret holes, and that someone small and quiet is needed. Ilse folds her arms and says no, as politely as she can.
Captain Brae does not argue, and she puts a card on the desk that says Pier Nine, midnight tomorrow. She leaves the old map behind as well, then walks back out into the rain.
In the morning a clerk in a grey coat arrives with a printed notice from the Harbour Lord. Every map shop must now pay a huge licence fee, and Ilse cannot afford even a tenth of it.

Ilse packs a tin of tea, her best pencils and three pairs of thick socks, and she tells herself she is only going to look. Then she locks her shop and walks to the harbour with her heart beating hard.
At the end of Pier Nine, a patched barge called Gull's Patience bobs beside a single lantern. A broad man on the deck waves at Ilse as if she were an old friend.
The big man is Fenwick, the cook, and he presses a hot bun into her hands. A girl with oily fingers, Tamsin Pike, proudly shows her the small steam engine that she keeps running.
The navigator, Barnaby Hatch, is nearly blind, but he sniffs the air and names the tide and the wind. He tells Ilse that he has not needed a chart in forty years.
Tamsin puts out the engine fire, and the barge drifts silently past the Harbour Lord's patrol boat. Ilse lies under a stiff canvas and does not dare to breathe.
At dawn the Whisperreef rises out of the sea, a forest of pale stones that seem to whisper in the wind. Between them lie narrow channels, and Barnaby says that they change with every tide.
Ilse lifts the thief's map to the rising sun, and the tiny holes throw a pattern of light across the deck. She follows the dots with her finger and finds a hidden path called the Old Channel.

A bank of fog called the Grey Breath rolls over the barge, and soon nobody can see the bow from the stern. Ilse reads the map by lantern and calls out turns, while Barnaby listens to the whispers on the stones.
Glowing lamp-eels come streaming toward the lantern and begin to bump and rock the barge. Ilse remembers a note in the map's corner, and she tells Fenwick to cover the light at once.
Ahead stands the Tide-Gate, a huge stone arch that opens only at low tide, and it is still shut. Captain Brae paces the deck, because every minute of waiting is a minute of danger.
Just as the water starts to fall, a fast patrol cutter appears in the mist with the Harbour Lord's flag. It is chasing them, and the Tide-Gate is still not open.
Ilse notices one pinhole off to the side of the Old Channel, where nobody else would look. It marks a gap between two rocks barely wide enough for the barge, and she asks the captain to trust her.
The barge scrapes through the secret passage with only a hand's breadth to spare on each side. Behind them the cutter swings wide, hits a sandbar, and sticks there with its crew shouting.
On a sandbar that night, Ilse admits that she has never been so frightened in her life. Captain Brae answers that she is frightened too, because her own mother is hungry on Kettle Island.
By afternoon they can see Skerry Hollow, a black rock with the Glass Tower rising from its top. Its mirrored windows flash in the sun like a hundred watching eyes.
The map shows a small drain door at the foot of the tower, near the waterline. They decide that Ilse and Tamsin will row in at night, while the others wait on the barge.
The tide pulls hard at the little boat, and Ilse's hands soon blister from the oars. Tamsin laughs softly, steers them onto the rocks, and ties the boat to an iron ring.
The drain door is rusty and old, but Tamsin works at the lock with two thin wires. It clicks open, and the two girls crawl into a cold passage that smells of seaweed.
A narrow staircase winds up inside the tower, and Ilse counts the steps as she climbs. She sees a tiny mark on the map, and grabs Tamsin's coat just before she steps on a hollow stair.
At the top of the stairs a great hall opens, and metal herons stalk across the floor with a steady click. Whenever one of them hears a sound, its head turns and its glass eye glows.
Ilse takes off her boots and gives Tamsin a pair of her thick woollen socks. Together they creep across the marble floor, between the herons, without making a sound.
In the highest room the Moon Atlas lies on a stand under a glass cover. A ring of tiny silver bells hangs around it, and each one is tied to a thin wire.
With her steadiest fingers, Ilse ties a loop of silk thread around each clapper, one by one. It takes her an hour, and Tamsin does not breathe once.
They lift the glass cover and open the Moon Atlas, but its pages are blank under the lamp. Ilse touches the paper and realises that the ink must show only in moonlight.
Ilse decides that they must take the whole book, because a copy made by candle would be blank anyway. She and Tamsin wrap it in a cloth sling and heave it between them.
A light appears at the bottom of the stairs, and heavy footsteps start to climb. It is Corvin Ashgrove himself, who has come to read his Atlas by the light of the full moon.
Corvin Ashgrove walks into the room and sees the empty stand. His furious shout echoes down the tower, and every Warden Heron lifts its head at once.
Ilse and Tamsin race down the spiral stairs with the heavy book, and the herons clatter behind them. At the forty-first step Ilse jumps high, and Tamsin follows her without a word.
Tamsin slams the iron door and wedges it with her spanner, and the two of them tumble into the little boat. They row back to the barge as hard as they can, while a lamp bobs behind them.
Ilse opens the book on the deck, and the moonlight makes the pages shine with silver lines. Every channel in the Whisperreef appears at once, along with the way the tide will move it.
The Harbour Lord's boat is faster than the barge, and soon he calls across the water. He offers Ilse a high post and plenty of gold, if she will only give him the book.
Ilse shakes her head and tells the Harbour Lord that a map belongs to everyone who has to cross the water. For once in her life, her voice does not tremble at all.
Following the Atlas, the barge reaches the Tide-Gate at the very moment it opens. The old arch grinds shut behind them, and the Harbour Lord's boat must wait there for the next tide.
At dawn the green hump of Kettle Island rises from the sea, and a crowd stands on the pier. The islanders are thin and tired, but they wave when they see the patched barge.
Captain Brae jumps onto the pier and wraps her arms around a small grey-haired woman. It is her mother, who is thin and tired but safe and very happy.
Ilse knows that a single book on a single barge cannot save an island. She sets up a table on the pier and begins to copy the channels onto many sheets, while the islanders bring her paper.
In four days the islanders make hundreds of copies, and every fishing boat carries one. A grain ship from the mainland takes the Old Channel and reaches Kettle Island at last.
At last the Harbour Lord arrives with a row of guards and demands his Atlas. The islanders stand shoulder to shoulder on the pier and say nothing at all.
Ilse holds up a copy and says that the charts are free to anyone who sails. The ship captains agree with her, and the Harbour Lord can no longer sell passage through the reef.
Back in Lanternhaven, Ilse finds that the licence fee has been cancelled for every map shop. Mistress Pim hugs her at the door, and the whole street seems to know her name.
Ilse puts up a new sign that says her maps are free to cross by, and she sits down with her tea. Then Captain Brae knocks with another old map, and Ilse sighs and reaches for her socks.
C1C2: Rain streamed down the window of a narrow shop in Lanternhaven, where Ilse Quill bent over a torn map with a brush no thicker than an eyelash. She hummed under her breath, content as a cat, for the rip was nearly closed and the ink had never run. Nothing in the whole world pleased her more than the sight of a neatly mended edge drying on the blotter.

Ilse had arranged her life as carefully as she arranged her pens, with tea at four, supper at six and the door locked before the lamps were lit. She had never sailed, never climbed a mountain and never been farther than the market on the hill. Adventures, she liked to say, were simply troubles that other people chose to go looking for, and she had no wish to join them.

Mistress Pim, the baker from next door, arrived with a warm loaf and a worried face, for she had heard bad news at the quay. No boat had come from Kettle Island in weeks, she said, and now flour cost twice what it had at midsummer. Ilse murmured something kind, thanked her for the bread, and did not give it another thought.

Late that afternoon the door flew open, letting in a gust of rain and a tall woman whose coat was stiff with dried salt. She introduced herself as Captain Odalys Brae, set a brittle roll of paper on the desk, and said that she had been told Ilse Quill was the best map-mender in the city. Ilse, who disliked dripping, said only that the captain was standing on her mat.

Holding the brittle paper to the lamp, Ilse noticed that it was pricked with hundreds of tiny holes, each one no bigger than a grain of sand. They were too exact to be accidents, and too secret to belong to any honest chart, for a thief had surely made them to find the way in the dark. The captain nodded, pleased, and said that this was the work of Jory Lightfoot, the most famous burglar who ever lived.

Between the harbour and Kettle Island lay the Whisperreef, the captain said, a maze of stone teeth where the channels moved with every tide and only one book could tell a ship where to go. That book, the Moon Atlas, belonged to Corvin Ashgrove, the Harbour Lord, who sold safe passage to anyone who could afford his price and let the rest go hungry. Her own island, she added in a flat voice, could not afford it any longer.

Only a mender could read the holes, the captain explained, and only someone small, quiet and patient could follow them into the Harbour Lord's tower and out again. She asked, plainly and without any flattery, whether Ilse Quill would come with them when the barge sailed. Ilse refused in the firmest voice she owned, and she added that she did not even like boats.

The captain did not argue, which was somehow a good deal worse than if she had shouted at the top of her voice. She laid a plain card on the desk, with Pier Nine and midnight tomorrow written in a firm hand, then left the pinholed map beside it and stepped out into the rain. The bell over the door jangled once, and the shop seemed much too quiet.

At eight o'clock the next morning a clerk in a grey coat presented Ilse with a printed notice that bore the Harbour Lord's seal. Every shop that sold or mended charts, it announced, must pay a new licence fee, a sum so large that Ilse could have worked ten years without earning it. She read it twice, found no mistake, and felt something stubborn stir behind her ribs.

She packed her tea tin, her finest pencils, a pot of paste and three pairs of thick woollen socks, telling herself all the while that she was only going to look. Then she locked the shop, slipped the key under her collar, and set off through the sleeping streets, starting at every shadow. By the time she reached the waterfront her hands were shaking, but her feet had not once turned back.

At the end of Pier Nine, beneath a lantern swinging in the wind, lay a barge so patched and mended that Ilse could not tell which of its planks were original. Its name, Gull's Patience, was painted on the bow in cheerful blue, and a mast stood crooked in the middle like a thumb. A very broad man on deck waved at her as though she were an old friend returning from a journey.

The broad man was Fenwick, the cook, who pressed a hot cinnamon bun into Ilse's hand and promised that she would not go hungry on his barge. A girl of about fifteen, with oil on her hands and a spanner behind one ear, introduced herself as Tamsin Pike and explained, with great pride, how she kept the barge's tiny steam engine alive using wire, spit and stubbornness. Ilse nodded politely and wondered, with some alarm, how anything so thoroughly held together by string could possibly float.

At the bow stood old Barnaby Hatch, the navigator, whose eyes had clouded over years ago and who sniffed the night air like a hound at a gate. He announced the tide, the wind and the very depth of the water beneath them, and then declared, without any boasting, that he had not needed a chart in forty years. Ilse found it a little alarming that someone so certain would still want her map.

Tamsin damped the engine until it hardly whispered, and the barge slid out of Lanternhaven on the ebb tide, its mast bare and its lamps hooded. A patrol boat passed so close that Ilse, lying rigid beneath a sheet of canvas, could hear the guards arguing over a card game. When the lights of the city had shrunk to a faint gold smear behind them, she finally remembered to breathe.

When the sun rose, the Whisperreef stood before them like the teeth of some drowned giant, pale and jagged, with the wind passing through its hollows in a long, soft murmur. Narrow channels of green water twisted between the stones, and Barnaby explained that every one of them would shift with the tide, so that a safe road at breakfast might be a grave by lunch. Ilse stared at the reef and understood at last why nobody crossed it without the Atlas.

Almost without thinking, Ilse lifted the thief's map toward the rising sun, and the pinpricks scattered a delicate pattern of light across the deck. She traced the glimmering dots with a finger and found, to her own astonishment, that they described a hidden road into the reef, which the old chart named the Old Channel. The crew fell silent, and Barnaby gave a slow, approving nod that Ilse would remember for the rest of her life.

Within an hour a wall of fog, which the old sailors called the Grey Breath, swallowed the barge so completely that nobody could see the bow from the stern. Ilse crouched beside the lantern with the map flat on her knees, calling out turns in a trembling voice, while Barnaby listened to the changing whispers on the stones and murmured corrections. Between the two of them, the barge crept forward through the grey like a needle through cloth.

Out of the murk came a stream of blue-glowing lamp-eels, drawn to the lantern like moths to a flame, and they began to butt the hull until the whole barge shuddered. Ilse remembered a tiny annotation in the corner of the thief's map, a drawing of a lantern with a line through it, and shouted for Fenwick to cover the light. He clapped a pot lid over it, the darkness fell, and the eels drifted away as mildly as a shoal of sleepy fish.

When the fog finally thinned they found themselves before the Tide-Gate, a great stone arch set across the channel, which opened only for a few minutes at the bottom of the tide. The water still stood too high, and Captain Brae paced the deck with her jaw set, for every minute of waiting was a minute in which the Harbour Lord's boats might find them. Ilse, who had spent her whole life waiting politely for things, was surprised to discover that she was the calmest person aboard.

Just as the water began to sink, a sleek cutter flying the Harbour Lord's flag burst out of the mist behind them, its oars flashing and its crew shouting orders. The Tide-Gate was still sealed and the barge had nowhere to run, and for a moment even Fenwick stopped chewing. Tamsin, however, was already feeding the engine, and the little funnel began to shake with smoke.

Ilse's eye, trained by years of reading the smallest marks, caught a single pinhole set apart from the others and pointing to a gap between two black rocks. It was barely wide enough for the barge, and no sensible sailor would have tried it, but she put her finger on the paper and asked the captain to trust her. Captain Brae looked at her for one long breath and then spun the wheel.

The barge scraped through the gap with scarcely a hand's breadth to spare on either side, while Tamsin held her breath and Barnaby counted the seconds under his own. Behind them the cutter, which had followed too eagerly, struck a sandbar the thief had marked long ago and stuck fast, its crew tumbling across the deck. Ilse began to laugh, a high shaky laugh she had never heard before, and could not stop for a full minute.

They anchored beside a low sandbar and lit a small fire, and Ilse, wrapped in a borrowed blanket, confessed that she had never been so frightened in all her life. The captain, staring at the flames, answered that she was frightened too, for her mother still lived on Kettle Island and had sent no word for a month. It was the first time Ilse understood that the journey was about people and not about paper.

By afternoon the barge reached Skerry Hollow, a lonely black rock out of which the Glass Tower rose in a slender spire of mirrored windows. Every pane flashed in the sun like an eye, and Ilse felt as if the whole building were watching the small barge creep toward it. Somewhere inside, she thought with a dry mouth, lay the book that a hungry island needed.

Spread on a crate, the thief's map revealed what no honest chart could, a small drain door at the foot of the tower, hidden just above the waterline and reached only at low tide. The crew agreed that Ilse, who could read the holes, and Tamsin, who could open any lock, would row ashore after dark while the captain, Fenwick and Barnaby waited with the barge. Ilse said that it was a thoroughly bad plan, and then she agreed to it.

The current tugged at the little boat as though it wanted to carry it back to the open sea, and Ilse's palms blistered after only a dozen strokes. Tamsin steered with a cheerful whisper of encouragement, and between them they brought the boat against the slippery rock and tied it to an old iron ring. Ilse, shaking and soaked, discovered that she was prouder of her blisters than she had ever been of her ink.

The drain door was rusty and slimy with weed, yet Tamsin coaxed its ancient lock with two slender wires and a murmured tune, until it surrendered with a faint click. The two of them crawled into a low passage that smelled of seaweed and cold stone, with water dripping somewhere in the dark. Ilse held the map close to her chest and whispered that the first turn was left.

A narrow staircase wound upward inside the tower, and Ilse counted the steps under her breath as she had counted so many lines of ink. Just before the forty-first she remembered a tiny cross near the thief's stairway, snatched Tamsin by the collar, and pointed to a plank that was painted to look like stone. Beneath it, when Tamsin dropped a coin, there was only a long, dark silence before the faint splash.

At the top of the stairs lay a great moonlit hall where a dozen metal herons patrolled on thin brass legs, each step marked by a precise, whirring click. The Warden Herons turned their long necks toward every sound, however small, and their glass eyes burned briefly red as they listened. Ilse pressed herself against a pillar and wondered how any thief, however famous, had ever walked through such a room.

Ilse drew off her boots, handed Tamsin a spare pair of her thick woollen socks, and whispered that this was what she had packed them for. Together they glided across the marble in perfect silence, slipping between two herons whose beaks swung past with a faint whirr only a few inches from their heads. Ilse had never been so grateful for her own good sense and her grandmother's knitting.

In the highest room of the tower the Moon Atlas rested on a carved stand beneath a glass cover, and around it hung a ring of tiny silver bells, each fastened to a hair-thin wire. If anyone lifted the glass, the wires would tug, the bells would ring, and the Warden Herons would come clattering up the stairs. Ilse looked at the bells for a long time, and the beginnings of an idea unfolded in her mind.

Ilse took out her finest silk thread and, with the same steady fingers that repaired torn maps, tied a tiny knot around the clapper of every silver bell. It took her nearly an hour, and Tamsin, who could not bear the tension, held a candle in both hands and bit her lip raw. When the last knot was tied, the whole ring of bells hung as mute as pebbles.

When they lifted the cover and turned the heavy pages, every leaf was blank, as white and silent as new snow. For a moment Ilse's heart sank, but then she touched the paper, noticed its faint silvery sheen, and understood that the ink must wake only under the light of the moon. That was why the Harbour Lord opened the book at his window once a month, and why nobody else could ever read it.

There was no time to copy anything, and a copy made by candlelight would have been blank in any case, so Ilse decided that the whole book must go with them. She and Tamsin wrapped it in a cloth sling, hoisted the great weight between them, and staggered toward the door like two people carrying a sleeping bear. Their stockinged feet made no noise at all on the cold stone, and the great weight swayed between them like a sleeping child.

Just as they reached the top of the stairs, a lamp swung into view below them, and a deep, unhurried tread began to climb. It was Corvin Ashgrove himself, in a long velvet cloak, who had come as he always did on the night of the full moon to read the secrets of his book. Ilse and Tamsin dived behind a heavy curtain, hugging the Atlas between them and praying that the cloth would not rustle.

The Harbour Lord strode into the room, stopped, and stared at the empty stand and the ring of silent, knotted bells, and for a long moment he said nothing at all. Then he roared with such fury that the glass trembled in its frames, and far below, a dozen mechanical herons snapped their heads up and began to stalk toward the stairs. Ilse felt Tamsin's hand close tightly on hers, and together they ran for the narrow door at the top of the stairs.

They plunged down the spiral stairs with the Atlas between them, the herons clattering and clicking at their backs like an avalanche of cutlery. At the forty-first step Ilse leapt, dragging Tamsin with her, and the herons, which knew nothing of false planks, crashed through it in a bright cascade of brass. The girls scarcely looked back as they tumbled, breathless and bruised, into the damp passage at the bottom of the tower.

Tamsin slammed the iron door behind them and jammed her spanner through the handle, and the two of them threw themselves into the little boat and rowed like people pursued by thunder. Behind them a great lantern was lowered into a fast boat, and a voice they knew all too well bellowed across the water. At the barge, Fenwick hauled them aboard with one enormous hand apiece, and Barnaby shouted that the tide was turning.

On the open deck, under a moon as round as a coin, Ilse laid back the cover of the Atlas, and the pages woke one by one with delicate lines of silver. Every channel of the Whisperreef bloomed before their eyes, with arrows for the tide and tiny notes for every shoal, and the crew gathered round in an awed circle. Barnaby, who could see none of it, said that he could smell the sea being made plain at last.

The Harbour Lord's boat was far quicker than the barge, and by midnight he was so close that Ilse could see the rings on his fingers as he cupped his hands to shout. He offered her a house in the best street in Lanternhaven, a salary beyond counting, and the title of Chief Mapmaker, if she would simply hand back the Atlas and forget the whole affair. It was, Ilse thought, the most tempting offer she had ever heard, and also the most insulting.

Ilse stood at the rail with the great book in her arms and, to her own surprise, spoke in a perfectly steady voice. A map, she said, is a promise to the next traveller, and nobody has the right to lock a promise in a tower and charge for it. She did not wait to hear his reply, but turned away and asked Barnaby for the next channel.

Guided by the silver lines, the barge reached the Tide-Gate at the exact minute the water fell low enough for the great arch to swing open. They shot through with an arm's length to spare, and behind them the old stones ground together with a boom that rolled across the reef. The Harbour Lord's boat, a heartbeat too late, was left drifting before a closed gate and a very long tide.

At dawn the green hump of Kettle Island lifted out of the sea, and on the end of its stone pier stood a crowd of thin, tired people, shading their eyes against the light. They had seen no vessel for so long that for a while nobody dared to cheer. Then someone recognised the crooked mast of the Gull's Patience, and the whole harbour began to shout.

Captain Brae leapt onto the pier before the barge had stopped moving and wrapped her arms around a small grey-haired woman in a patched shawl. It was her mother, thin and tired but quite safe, and for a long time neither of them spoke. Ilse, standing awkwardly on the deck with her hands clasped, discovered that her own eyes were wet as well.

A single book carried by a single barge, Ilse realised, could not feed a whole island, and she resolved to copy every channel for anyone who needed it. She set up a table on the pier in the moonlight, and the islanders, who understood at once, brought her paper, ink and every candle they owned. By midnight there were a dozen hands helping her, and the first neat copy was drying in the wind.

Within four days the islanders had produced hundreds of copies, each marked in careful silver ink and tucked into the cabin of every fishing boat in the harbour. Then, on the fifth morning, a grain ship from the mainland, whose captain had heard the news, nosed through the Old Channel with its hold full of flour and barley. The whole island came down to the quay to carry sacks, and Fenwick wept openly into a loaf.

On the eighth day the Harbour Lord sailed into the island's little harbour with four guards and a face like thunder, demanding that the stolen Atlas be handed over at once. The islanders, hundreds strong and holding copies of the charts in their hands, simply stood shoulder to shoulder on the pier and said nothing. It was, Ilse thought, the loudest silence she had ever heard in her whole quiet and careful life.

Ilse stepped forward, holding up one of her copies, and explained to the gathered ship captains that these charts were now in every cabin and could never be locked away again. The captains conferred briefly, voted to end the Harbour Lord's fee for ever, and told him to go home. Corvin Ashgrove looked at the crowd, looked at the paper, and understood at last that he had been outdrawn by a woman with a pot of paste.

When Ilse returned to Lanternhaven she found that the licence fee had been cancelled for every map shop in the city, and that her little street had hung out bunting in her honour. Mistress Pim flung her arms around her at the door, and neighbours she had never spoken to shook her hand and thanked her for something she scarcely understood. Ilse said that she had only done a bit of mending, and nobody believed her.

Ilse hung a new sign outside the shop, painted in her neatest hand, and settled at her desk with a pot of tea and a torn atlas that needed a gentle repair. She had barely stirred in the sugar when the bell jangled and Captain Brae appeared in the doorway, grinning, with another brittle roll of paper under her arm. Ilse sighed deeply, put down her cup, and went to find her thickest socks.
